papers.title: Asynchronous Distributed Variational Gaussian Processes for Regression
papers.abstract: Gaussian processes (GPs) are powerful non-parametric function estimators. However, their applications are largely limited by the expensive computational cost of the inference procedures. Existing stochastic or distributed synchronous variational inferences, although have alleviated this issue by scaling up GPs to millions of samples, are still far from satisfactory for real-world large applications, where the data sizes are often orders of magnitudes larger, say, billions. To solve this problem, we propose ADVGP, the first Asynchronous Distributed Variational Gaussian Process inference for regression, on the recent large-scale machine learning platform, PARAMETERSERVER. ADVGP uses a novel, flexible variational framework based on a weight space augmentation, and implements the highly efficient, asynchronous proximal gradient optimization. While maintaining comparable or better predictive performance, ADVGP greatly improves upon the efficiency of the existing variational methods. With ADVGP, we effortlessly scale up GP regression to a real-world application with billions of samples and demonstrate an excellent, superior prediction accuracy to the popular linear models.

papers.title: Fundamentals of Implant Dentistry
papers.abstract: This well-written, well-documented surgical-based implant publication is a sequel to its restorative-based predecessor (Volume I). Although implant dentistry has its roots well entrenched in restorative-based principles, the surgical elements play a vital and synergistic role in the overall success of each case. This book addresses how the surgical-based clinician plays a key role in treatment planning and in following through with successful surgical outcomes. The importance of a true interdisciplinary approach to implant dentistry is stressed throughout the book. The initial 4 chapters are devoted to the fundamental concepts and principles of implant dentistry and include the importance of the patient's medical and dental history in addition to the role of interdisciplinary treatment planning. Chapter 1 emphasizes the key role of the underlying concepts of osseointegration and its impact on implant-based reconstruction of the oral cavity. It also stresses the importance of the implant soft tissue interface and continuing evolution of CAD/CAM technologies along with the ever-evolving hard and soft tissue procedures that affect the overall case success. Chapter 2 covers the evaluation and advancements made in the field of implant surfaces that have resulted in more bioreactive elements. There is special coverage of methods that have been developed to improve clinical performance by increasing the wettability of the implant surfaces facilitating osteoconductivity between the implant surface and bone. Chapter 3 focuses on the importance of a thorough medical and dental history of all patients who are candidates for implant-based surgery. Special emphasis is made on risk factors as well as both relative and absolute contraindications for these procedures. Chapter 4 covers all the important topics of diagnostics and interdisciplinary treatment planning. There is special emphasis on the role of both the surgical-based and restorative-based clinician and their collaboration for successful outcomes. There is ample time spent discussing the basic workup and key diagnostic elements of both the partially edentulous and completely edentulous patient. Chapter 5 deals with basic surgical principles that are critical to successful outcomes. This well-organized approach covers the entire spectrum of implant placement in both partially edentulous and completely edentulous cases. Implant type, soft tissue management, flap design, osteotomy preparation, and soft tissue closure protocols are described in depth. Special attention is devoted to application of these surgical principles in the esthetic zone. Chapter 6 is devoted to computer-guided planning and surgery with emphasis on both semiguided and fully guided approaches for implant placement. The indications, advantages, and disadvantages along with issues of concern are adequately covered. In addition, both absolute and relative contraindications are described in detail. Clinical examination factors (for a fully guided approach), the overall computer-guided workup, design, and fabrication of a surgical template along with surgical protocols for fully guided and semiguided approaches are all well covered with excellent illustrations and clinical photographs. Chapter 7 provides the reader with a well-organized overview of the clinical application of tilted and zygomatic implants for surgical-based implant reconstruction of both terminal dentition and edentulous patients. The indications, contraindications, surgical, and prosthodontic workup along with the surgical protocol for tilted and zygomatic implants is well covered. In Chapter 8, the most current hard and soft tissue augmentation procedures used in implant dentistry are reviewed with the emphasis being on hard tissue procedures. The initial section covers the selection and comparative analysis of donor materials and includes intraoral and extraoral autografts, bone substitutes, and growth factors (rhBMP-2 and platelet concentrates). The second section on hard tissue augmentation covers specific surgical protocols, including lateral and crestal sinus grafting, autogenous bone blocks, particulate bone grafting, interpositional inlay bone grafting, ridge splitting, and alveolar distraction osteogenesis. The final section, although brief in content, includes surgical techniques of subepithelial connective tissue grafts, free gingival grafts, and papilla reconstruction. Chapter 9 deals with implant-based reconstruction of maxillary and mandibular defects. Reconstruction of the severely resorbed mandible is addressed with the description of an approach that involves a combination of autogenous bone harvested from the iliac crest along with HA particles. The severely resorbed maxilla is also reviewed and includes the various approaches, such as crestal onlay bone grafting, Le Fort I osteotomy with interpositional grafting, along with inlay grafting to the maxillary antrum and nasal floor. Next, reconstruction of major mandibular defects is addressed with a thorough description of the hybridized reconstruction technique approach. This novel protocol combines a fibula-free flap with tissue engineering. Finally, the VSP-assisted microvascular fibula-free flap reconstruction approach is described in detail to address maxillary defects. Chapter 10 addresses surgical considerations and strategies for the esthetic zone. The importance of a comprehensive and methodical approach to all esthetic zone cases is emphasized throughout this chapter, which is divided into 3 major sections. Section 1 deals specifically with the surgical evaluation and workup for the esthetic zone. It includes specific clinical examination findings specific to the esthetic zone, such as smile line and tooth display, maxilla mandibular relationships, bone and soft tissue levels adjacent to the natural dentition, occlusal plane and incisal plane and vertical dimension of occlusion, UCLA esthetic implant analysis, photographic documentation and diagnostic wax-up, and radiographic analysis of the esthetic zone. Section 2 deals with specific factors affecting clinical outcomes in the esthetic zone. This includes gingival biotype, the impact of immediate or delayed provisionalization on soft tissue contours, biologic width, ridge anatomy and contours and marginal tissue recession, impact of implant form design on bone and peri-implant tissue maintenance, impact of implant positioning on bone and soft tissue maintenance, impact of immediate loading/provisionalization of bone and soft tissue levels, impact of socket augmentation, socket preservation, and ridge preservation, impact of implant angulation and position, and impact of computer-guided treatment planning and surgical techniques. Section 3 deals with specific surgical procedures in the esthetic zone. Hard tissue grafting protocols are covered and include socket augmentation, ridge preservation techniques, vertical augmentation that includes autogenous bone block grafts, GBR with membrane, GBR with titanium mesh, interpositional inlay grafting, and distraction osteogenesis. Horizontal augmentation techniques include GBR, single-stage approach, 2-state approach, ridge expansion, and autogenous bone block grafting. Soft tissue techniques are also addressed that include soft tissue defects, multiple tooth defects, epithelial connective tissue grafting, subepithelial connective tissue grafting, and connective tissue grafts after implant placement. Finally, immediate implant placement on tooth extract is described in addition to immediate loading and immediate provisionalization. Chapter 11 deals with immediate loading, immediate provisionalization, and delayed loading. This chapter is divided into 9 sections and is very descriptive of immediate loading in general. It begins with definitions of immediate loading, immediate provisionalization, early loading, delayed loading, and progressive loading. Important issues to consider for immediate loading or immediate provisionalization include chronic periodontitis, periodontal biotype, implant anchorage, immobilization of the implant during healing, cross-arch stabilization, implants placed into fresh extraction sites, experience and skill of the implant team, smile line, control of occlusal factors, opposing arch dentition as well as minimalizing cantilever lengths and the impact of acute periapical and periodontal infections along with parafunctional activity and various jaw forms, and patient compliance. Next, specific issues to consider during patient selection are described for the edentulous mandible and include bone density and quantity, jaw relations, arch form and anterior loop of the inferior alveolar nerve, status of the opposing arch, zone of attached keratinized tissue, lip and facial support, interocclusal space, and finally compliance. Regarding the edentulous maxilla, sinus pneumatization and implant distribution patterns are considered, along with patterns of resorption, esthetics, and implant biomechanics, lip line, speech articulation and hygiene access, jaw relations, status of the opposing arch, thickness of the mucoperiosteum in the anterior region, interocclusal space, and compliance in this section. With the partially edentulous patients, important parameters parafunctional activity, various jaw forms, residual ridge architecture, interocclusal space, compliance, opposing arch configuration, and finally occlusion are covered in detail. The next major section involves the esthetic zone and includes single-tooth defects along with a variety of other parameters that are addressed in detail. The next major section is single-tooth molar defects and includes immediate placement and loading for both mandibular and maxillary molars. Posterior quadrants with extended edentulous sites are then covered in both arches. The next major section includes relative contraindications to immediate loading for both edentulous and partially edentulous patients. The surgical and prosthodontic workup for immediate loading/provisionalization is covered quite well in both edentulous and partially edentulous patients. Next, selection of implants for immediate loading is detailed, followed by osteotomy preparation and insertion of the implant as well as assessment of implant anchorage. Finally, prosthodontic use is addressed as well. Chapter 12 deals with maintenance and follow-up. This is the most important chapter that emphasizes the importance of patients treated with osseointegrated implants be very closely followed. It is imperative that the health of the bone and soft tissues associated with the implants be closely monitored along with the prosthesis that should be carefully evaluated on a regular basis to ensure appropriate function. During the follow-up evaluations, it is important that both the medical and dental histories be updated, as well as plaque levels, soft tissue health, and implant bone levels. The prosthesis itself should be very meticulously examined to ensure that appropriate occlusal relationships have been maintained. Finally, patients with peri-implant mucositis and peri-implantitis should be treated accordingly. In addition, any deficiencies associated with the prosthesis itself secondary to wear, chipping, and fracture should be addressed. Chapter 13 deals specifically with surgical complications of implant placement. It is divided into 2 main sections. It begins with intraoperative complications that include lack of primary stability, implants placed too close together, perforations of the facial plate of bone, perforation of the lingual plate of the mandible and bleeding, perforation of the inferior border of the mandible, injury to the inferior alveolar nerve, mental nerve, or lingual nerve, fracture of the mandible, damage to the implant platform during placement, damage to the internal threads of the implant, penetration of the apex of an implant into the maxillary sinus, tearing of the sinus membrane during sinus augmentation, excessive bleeding during sinus augmentation, loss of an implant or graft material into the maxillary sinus, postoperative maxillary sinusitis, ingestion and aspiration of different implant component parts and instrumentation, implant displacement or migration into the floor of the mouth or infratemporal fossa. The second major section deals with postoperative complications, such as excessive facial placement or inclination of the implants, bisphosphonate-related osteonecrosis, devitalization of adjacent dentition, improper apical coronal positioning, exposure of titanium mesh, exposure of membranes and graft material, exposure of buried implants, overheating of the apical portion of the implant site during implant site preparation, and finally peri-implant mucositis or implantitis.

papers.title: Reactive scoliosis: a challenging phenomenon in adolescent patients with hip arthritis
papers.abstract: Functional limb length discrepancy (LLD) in adolescents can result from soft tissue contracture following long-standing hip disease. We present a case of a 13-year-old girl with difficulty in ambulation due to right hip pain and LLD. Radiographs revealed severe arthritis of right hip with signs of avascular necrosis of the femoral head. The patient had developed reactive scoliosis of lumbar spine along with pelvic obliquity. After failing conservative management, total hip arthroplasty (THA) without attempting to equalize LLD was performed. At 6-month follow-up, patient was pain free with full range of motion and her functional LLD was completely resolved. In such adolescent patients, reactive scoliosis of spine is reversible, and with no evidence of true LLD, THA without correcting LLD should be the right choice.

papers.title: Kemampuan Pemecahan Masalah Melalui Pembelajaran Interactive Demonstration Siswa Kelas X SMA pada Materi Kalor
papers.abstract: The application of teacher centered learning in classroom is causing the underdevelopment of students problem solving ability and students activity in learning. Interactive demonstration is an active learning model developed by Wenning. Through interactive demonstrations, students can use the basic intellectual process skills that includes predicting, explaining, estimating, acquiring and processing data, formulating and revising scientific explanations using logic and evidence, and recognizing and analyzing alterative xplanations and models. The purpose of this research is to determine the effect of interactive learning demonstration toward students' problem solving ability. This research was mixed method research with embedded design. The sample is selected by purposive sampling method, that was the grade X MIA 1 students of SMAN 1 Bangil. The results of this study indicate that there is the effect of interactive demonstration learning and that learning can enhance students' problem-solving abilities.

papers.title: Two-component thermosensitive hydrogels: Phase separation affecting rheological behavior
papers.abstract: Extracellular matrices are mainly composed of a mixture of different biopolymers and therefore the use of two or more building blocks for the development of tissue-mimicking hydrogels is nowadays an attractive strategy in tissue-engineering. Multi-component hydrogel systems may undergo phase separation, which in turn can lead to new, unexpected material properties. The aim of this study was to understand the role of phase separation on the mechanical properties and 3D printability of hydrogels composed of triblock copolymers of polyethylene glycol (PEG) and methacrylated poly(N-(2-hydroxypropyl) methacrylamide-mono/dilactate) (pHPMAlac) blended with methacrylated hyaluronic acid (HAMA). To this end, hydrogels composed of different concentrations of PEG/pHPMAlac and HAMA, were analyzed for phase behavior and rheological properties. Subsequently, phase separation and rheological behavior as function of the two polymer concentrations were mathematically processed to generate a predictive model. Results showed that PEG/pHPMAlac/HAMA hydrogels were characterized by hydrophilic, HAMA-richer internal domains dispersed in a more hydrophobic continuous phase, composed of PEG/ pHPMAlac, and that the volume fraction of the dispersed phase increased by increasing HAMA concentration. Storage modulus, yield stress and viscosity increased with increasing HAMA concentration for low/medium HAMA contents (0.75% w/w), while a further increase of HAMA resulted in a decrease of the mentioned properties. On the other hand, by increasing the concentration of PEG/pHPMAlac these rheological properties were enhanced. The generated models showed a good fitting with experimental data, and were used to identify an exemplary 3D printability window for PEG/pHPMAlac/HAMA hydrogels, which was verified by rheological characterization and preparation of 3D printed scaffolds. In conclusion, a clear relationship between phase separation and rheological behavior in these two-component hydrogels can be described by complex functions of the two polymer concentrations. The predictive model generated in this study can be used as a valid tool for the identification of hydrogel compositions with desired, selected characteristics.
